Chapter Three: Family, Grief, and the Struggle to Find Answers Far from Home
When someone you love goes missing, your whole world shrinks down to one thing—finding them. That’s exactly what happened to Lucie’s family. In the days after she disappeared, everything was a blur: fear, hope, frustration, all tangled together. And with Lucie so far away in Japan, while they were back in England, every phone call felt like it carried the weight of the world.
Her dad, Tim Blackman, landed in Tokyo absolutely determined to bring Lucie home. Not long after, her sister Sophie joined him. Later, Lucie’s mom Jane arrived too. Each of them brought their own strengths and struggles to this impossible search. Tim was practical, laser-focused, not willing to settle for easy answers. Sophie, though younger, was just as determined. And Jane—already separated from Tim—now had to navigate not just her grief, but the tension that comes from searching for a child with an ex-partner.
Very quickly, they realized just how tough it was to get answers far from home. The Japanese police? They were polite, but also a bit distant, and their way of working just felt... slow. Whenever the family tried to push for more action, it sometimes made things worse, straining their relationship with the authorities. Add in the language barrier, and it made every conversation feel like climbing a mountain. Cultural differences only made things more confusing.
Then came the media storm. Journalists from all over the globe flooded Tokyo, hungry for every detail. Some reporters truly cared, but others were just after the most sensational angle. Suddenly, the family found themselves in the spotlight, every move watched, every word picked apart. They kept giving interviews, hoping someone out there might have a clue, but it was absolutely exhausting.
As weeks passed, the pressure started to crack the family’s unity. Old wounds reopened, and working together became harder. Tim and Jane struggled to see eye to eye, their differences only magnified by stress and heartbreak. Sophie tried desperately to hold everyone together, but the strain was overwhelming. Even with friends and supporters rallying around, the sense of isolation was hard to shake.
The search for Lucie turned into a full-time job. The family ran their own investigations, chased leads the police hadn’t followed up, hired private detectives, put up flyers, met anyone who might know something—anything. Each day brought a fresh wave of hope... and disappointment.
People in Japan watched the story unfold with a mix of sympathy and curiosity. Some admired how fiercely the family fought, but others just saw them as outsiders who didn’t really get how things worked there. The way grief was expressed became a big difference—Lucie’s family wore their emotions on their sleeves, while many Japanese people were much more reserved. Sometimes, that passion was misunderstood as aggression, leading to even more confusion.
Through all of this, the family held on tightly to hope—that Lucie was still out there, alive. Giving up just wasn’t an option. The search became their way of coping, of keeping their hearts and minds busy, because standing still was simply unbearable.
And in those quiet moments, the harsh reality crept in. They had to face the possibility that Lucie might never come home. Grief became a constant shadow, but so did resilience. They learned to lean on each other—finding strength in even the smallest victories, and pushing forward, no matter how uncertain the road ahead looked.
This experience changed them in ways they never expected. They saw both the very best and the very worst in people—the kindness of total strangers, and the coldness of big institutions. They realized that closure isn’t just a finish line you cross. It’s a journey. Sometimes, searching for answers becomes just as important as the answers themselves.
